request.system: You are a senior clinical coder in an Australian public hospital with fifteen years of experience coding inpatient episodes in ICD-10-AM. You are careful, conservative, and you never invent a code you are not sure of the chapter for.

messages.content:
Code the episode of care below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed. Give the three-character ICD-10-AM category for the principal diagnosis.

Hospital course:
Patient Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Patient Name]
Admission Date: [Admission Date]
Discharge Date: [Discharge Date]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital due to lower extremity swelling and pain for four days. Physical examination revealed left lower limb pitting edema and calf tenderness. Color Doppler ultrasound showed an extensive DVT affecting the common iliac, external iliac and common femoral vein as well as superficial femoral down to popliteal vein. Treatment included bed rest, elevation with bandaging of left leg, and low molecular weight heparin injections. Investigations revealed no underlying etiology. Abdominal and pelvic US and CT scan showed an impacting stone and a severe left hydroureteronephrosis with almost lost of cortical thickness. Percutaneous nephrostomy was performed to decompress the hydronephrotic kidney. JJ stent was inserted and subsequently removed. Six weeks later, Doppler US showed complete recanalization of the superficial femoral, popliteal as well as the proximal segment of deep veins of the leg but common iliac, external iliac and common femoral veins and proximal superficial femoral vein were still partially thrombosed. Through pneumatic lithotripsy, the stone was fragmented under spinal anesthesia. Three months after that, Doppler US showed complete recanalization of iliac vessels.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:
Treatment included bed rest, elevation with bandaging of left leg, and low molecular weight heparin injections. Percutaneous nephrostomy was performed to decompress the hydronephrotic kidney. JJ stent was inserted and subsequently removed. Pneumatic lithotripsy was performed to fragment the stone under spinal anesthesia. The patient was discharged on oral anticoagulation in the form of rivaroxaban 20 mg daily.

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to have regular follow-up visits with their healthcare provider.

Signed by: [Healthcare Provider Name and Title]

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
Principal diagnosis: the admission was for left lower limb swelling and pain, and the cause was an extensive left lower limb DVT (iliofemoral, femoral and popliteal veins). Investigation found an obstructing ureteric stone with severe hydroureteronephrosis. This is probably the underlying cause, through venous compression or a prothrombotic state, though the summary states "no underlying etiology" for the DVT. The DVT was the reason for admission, and it was treated first with heparin and then rivaroxaban. The stone was treated too, with nephrostomy and lithotripsy, but the clinical picture and presenting problem point to the DVT.

The category for deep vein thrombosis of the lower limb is I80 (phlebitis and thrombophlebitis) in ICD-10-AM. Acute DVT of the femoral vein is I80.1, and of other deep vessels of the lower extremities is I80.2. Both sit under I80. The other candidate, calculus of the ureter, falls under N20.

Counterargument: the stone and hydronephrosis needed the most procedures (nephrostomy, stent, lithotripsy). Even so, the condition chiefly responsible for the admission after study is the DVT, which was the reason for admission and was treated throughout. The urological procedures were secondary findings, and the stone was addressed later in the course.

CODE: I80
